paper_title: T3lescope: Arbitrary-Resolution High-Fidelity Generative Surface Reconstruction from Images

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We reconstruct high-fidelity 3D scene meshes from posed multi-view images without per-scene optimization, across scales ranging from single objects to large outdoor scenes. Per-scene optimization methods lack the learned 3D prior needed when observations are sparse or surfaces are glossy or transparent. Existing generative methods leverage such priors to complete geometry in sparsely observed regions, but typically operate at a fixed resolution over a limited spatial extent, trading spatial coverage against detail. Reconstructing a large scene therefore often requires partitioning it into independently processed overlapping local regions, making it difficult to maintain global geometric consistency. To address these issues, we propose T3lescope, which applies a single fixed-resolution generator across scene scales in an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade. A coarse level establishes the scene layout, and finer levels perturb and denoise geometry inherited from the coarser level within progressively finer spatial cells to recover surface detail. The model is trained on individual cells at multiple scales and shares its weights across all levels, so no hierarchy is fixed during training, and the number of levels, cell scales, and cell locations are determined at inference time. On indoor, outdoor, and city-scale scenes, T3lescope outperforms feed-forward and generative baselines, matches or surpasses per-scene optimization, and recovers fine structures as well as glossy and transparent surfaces. These results show that our method generalizes across diverse scenes, view counts, and image resolutions. Project page: https://pfnet-research.github.io/t3lescope/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Reconstructing high-fidelity 3D meshes from posed multi-view images is important for broad range of real-world applications, including robotic perception, simulation, digital twins, and immersive environments. These applications require both fine surface detail and globally consistent scene geometry, across targets ranging from single objects to large outdoor scenes. Existing approaches broadly fall into three categories: per-scene optimization, feed-forward prediction, and generative reconstruction. Optimization-based methods fit scene-specific 3D representation to the input images and can recover accurate surfaces from dense observations (Wang et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024; Guedon et al., 2025). However, they require optimization for every scene and, lacking learned 3D prior, fail under sparse views, occlusion, or glossy, reflective, and transparent surfaces. Feed-forward methods address the cost of per-scene optimization by learning priors across many scenes and directly predicting geometry such as depth or point maps (Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Keetha et al., 2026). However, their outputs are typically image-aligned and must be fused across views to form complete mesh, where cross-view inconsistencies can introduce noise, holes, or duplicate surfaces. Generative reconstruction addresses both issues by conditioning learned 3D generator on the input views. Like feed-forward methods, it avoids per-scene optimization, while its learned prior directly predicts complete 3D representation, including weakly constrained surfaces (Xiang et al., 2025; 2026). Its main limitation is scale: current 3D generators typically operate on fixed voxel grid at single scene scale, trading spatial coverage against geometric detail. GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026), the closest prior work, extends such fixed-resolution generator to large scenes using overlapping local cells with MultiDiffusion (Bar-Tal et al., 2023). While this increases spatial coverage, distant regions interact only indirectly through overlaps, making global geometry difficult to maintain. Coarse-to-fine 3D generators offer another solution, but existing approaches fix their hierarchy, spatial extent, and output resolution during training (Ren et al., 2024a;b). These limitations motivate different question: can single fixed-resolution generator be composed across scene scales at inference time, from global structure to progressively finer detail? To this end, we propose T3lescope, an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade that reuses the same generator across multiple scene scales. coarse level reconstructs the full scene and establishes its global structure, while each finer level refines inherited geometry by halving the cell size, perturbing it with noise, and denoising it to recover finer surface detail. The same weights are shared across all levels and trained on individual cells at multiple scene scales, without paired coarse-to-fine supervision. Thus, cell size, layout, and cascade depth determine spatial coverage and output resolution at inference time. This flexibility, however, makes image conditioning nontrivial: cells vary in position and physical scale across scenes and cascade levels, while each level requires image features at different resolution. To address this, we precompute reusable multi-resolution image features and condition each voxel using its projected location and projected size. This makes conditioning independent of absolute scene position and scale, allowing cells to be placed at arbitrary positions and scales while providing the detail required at each cascade level. We evaluate T3lescope on two public benchmarks, ScanNet++ and Tanks and Temples, and on our own city-block dataset, under both sparseand dense-view settings. It outperforms feed-forward and generative baselines and is competitive with per-scene optimization. It recovers fine structures as well as glossy and transparent surfaces. Results also show that our method generalizes across diverse scenes, view counts, and image resolutions (Figures 1 and 3). Ablations validate both parent initialization and image conditioning. Our contributions are: We propose an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade that reuses one fixed-resolution 3D generator across scene scales, with coverage and resolution chosen at inference time. We develop cell-independent multi-scale conditioning scheme that reuses image features across cells, levels, and sampling steps while allowing flexible cell placement and scale.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Mesh reconstruction. Mesh reconstruction from posed images has traditionally relied on multiview stereo, which matches pixels across images and fuses the recovered geometry (Schonberger et al., 2016). Neural implicit and Gaussian-based methods instead optimize 3D representation for each scene (Wang et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Guedon et al., 2025; Gomez et al., 2026), with recent methods scaling to city-scale scenes (Liu et al., 2025). These approaches recover accurate geometry from dense views and can be regularized with learned monocular or geometric cues. However, they require per-scene optimization and tend to degrade under sparse observations or with challenging glossy and transparent surfaces. Feed-forward methods instead learn scene priors that generalize to unseen scenes and predict image-aligned depth or point maps in single forward pass (Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Keetha et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025). While they avoid per-scene optimization, their predictions must be fused across views, making the resulting mesh sensitive to cross-view inconsistencies. In contrast, our method directly generates the mesh with 3D generator, without either per-scene optimization or multi-view fusion. Generative 3D reconstruction. Recent 3D generative models directly produce high-resolution meshes through sparse structures and structured latents (Xiang et al., 2026). Pixel-aligned image conditioning improves geometric fidelity via explicit 2D3D correspondence (Li et al., 2026a). GenRecon extends an object-level 3D generator to scene-scale reconstruction by tiling the scene with local overlapping cells and jointly sampling them with MultiDiffusion (Schmid et al., 2026; Bar-Tal et al., 2023). This extends generation beyond the models native spatial extent, but each denoiser operates on local cell, and distant regions interact only indirectly through neighboring overlaps. Instead, our cascade propagates global structure from the coarse reconstruction to each finer cell. Hierarchical generation. Coarse-to-fine 3D generators reach high resolution with hierarchies whose levels and scales are fixed during training, often with separate model at each level (Ren et al., 2024a;b; Meng et al., 2025). Methods for larger scenes scale spatial extent by progressively extending the generated region (Wu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Meng et al., 2026). In 2D, cascaded diffusion models similarly train separate model for each resolution (Ho et al., 2022), while training-free methods reuse the same model to progressively refine upsampled samples (Meng et al., 2022; Du et al., 2024). We adapt this idea to 3D. At each finer level, we reduce the cell size while keeping the generator resolution fixed. This allows the same model to be reused across scales, with the hierarchy configured at inference time.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: We reconstruct mesh from posed multi-view images with 3D generative model, without perscene optimization. Since the generator has fixed resolution, we reconstruct the scene coarse-tofine. The coarsest level captures the scene, and finer levels refine it (Section 3.2). At each level, we partition the scene into overlapping cells (Section 3.1) and apply the generator with corresponding image features (Section 3.4). We train single model across scales (Section 3.3) and configure the hierarchy and spatial scale at inference time. Figure 2 shows the pipeline.

sections.title: 3.1 SINGLE-LEVEL SCENE GENERATION
sections.content: We adopt TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026), sparse-voxel mesh generator, as our generative model. It first generates the sparse structure (SS) of surface voxels and then generates mesh over that structure. We refer to these two steps as the SS and mesh stages. The input is set of posed images = {(Ii, Ki, Ti)}N i=1, where Ii is an RGB image, Ki its intrinsics, and Ti its camera pose. Both stages use 3D VAEs to encode their representations and Diffusion Transformers (Peebles & Xie, 2023) for flow matching. The generator operates on fixed R3 sparse voxel grid and is conditioned on DINOv3 (Simeoni et al., 2025) image features together with camera intrinsics and poses. The parameter ts controls the trade-off between preserving the parent geometry and incorporating finer image details available at the child level. As ts 0, the child remains close to the parent. As ts 1, it relies mainly on local high-resolution image features and loses the global context that the parent provides. The global context helps resolve ambiguities that cannot be determined from single cell alone. To balance local detail and global context, we set ts = 0.8 empirically for all benchmarks, without tuning per scene, dataset, or view count. The parent also determines the child-cell layout by retaining only cells that intersect its predicted geometry, restricting generation to relevant regions. To initialize the cells of the coarsest level and per-cell view selection, we use the point cloud from Depth Anything 3 (DA3) (Lin et al., 2026). We use the depth only for these two choices, and never fuse it into the output geometry (Appendix D.3).

sections.title: 3.3 MULTI-SCALE TRAINING OF A SHARED MODEL
sections.content: Since the parent prediction is used only to initialize the next level at inference time via Equation 1, training does not require paired coarse and fine examples. We train one SS flow and one mesh flow on individual cells, using standard conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). We map cells of several edge lengths to the same canonical coordinates and R3 grid and condition the model on the images that observe each cell. Cells at different scales therefore differ only in voxel spacing = s/R. Neither nor is given to the model, so the same weights apply across scales. Unlike XCube and SCube (Ren et al., 2024a;b), our hierarchy is not fixed during training, so its depth, cell layout, and physical scales can be chosen at inference time without retraining. Appendix provides more details about training.

sections.title: 3.4 CELL-INDEPENDENT MULTI-SCALE IMAGE CONDITIONING
sections.content: In the MultiDiffusion formulation above, every cell is evaluated at every flow step of the SS and mesh stages, making feature reuse important for efficient inference. Pixel-aligned conditioning (Li et al., 2026a; Schmid et al., 2026) projects each voxel into the input views, bilinearly samples one feature per view, and aggregates them before the 3D generator. However, the DINOv3 token grid is coarse, so the sampled features can lose the information needed for detailed surface reconstruction. Pixal3D (Li et al., 2026a) addresses this by upsampling features to image resolution, but the upsampled maps become costly to cache as image resolution and view count increase, and must then be recomputed at every flow step. Aggregating before the generator also keeps the view weights from depending on the current voxel state. We address these with voxel-queried image attention over compact cached features and cell-independent tile bank that provides each cell with scale-matched image features without per-cell encoding. Voxel-queried image attention. For voxel p, we gather the DINO tokens within window around its projection in each view, and let the current voxel feature hp attend to all of them with single softmax over tokens and views. Instead of bilinear sampling, we apply relative positional encoding to the continuous offset from the voxel projection to the token center to preserve subtoken position and local image context. As the query is the current voxel feature, the attention weights adapt to the evolving 3D state across transformer blocks and flow steps. We also encode the projected voxel size and ray direction (Li et al., 2025) (Appendix D.1). For finer detail, the mesh stage also samples compact multi-stride ConvNeXt features (Liu et al., 2022) at the same projected location. The DINO features remain on their native token grid, while the ConvNeXt features are lightweight, allowing both to be cached for all views and reused across cells and flow steps. Cell-independent tile bank. The base generator (Xiang et al., 2026) is pretrained on 512 512 images that frame the target region at particular image scale. To match this pretraining setup, each view should provide crop that covers the cell projection, with pixel spacing matched to the cells voxel spacing. GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026) instead resizes each full image to single resolution. In wide scenes, where an image covers large area, this can leave fine cell with only few pixels. Instead of center-cropping the images around each cell projection, which would require separate image encoding for every cellview pair and dominate the cost, we build an isotropic pyramid for each input image and divide each level into fixed grid of 512 512 tiles (Figure 2(b)). Each tile is defined by its source image, pyramid level, and crop origin, independently of the 3D cells. sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models and training data. We train two models (Appendix E): general scene reconstruction model and city-block reconstruction model. We initialize both from pretrained TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026) model, first fine-tune it for multi-view conditioning on TexVerse (Zhang et al., 2025), and then fine-tune the two models independently on their respective datasets. The general model is trained exclusively on synthetic data: the single-room datasets SAGE-10K (Xia et al., 2026) and 3D-FRONT (Fu et al., 2021), together with our procedurally generated multi-room houses and grass scenes. The city-block model is fine-tuned on our dataset of photographs captured in Japanese cities and their paired building information models (BIMs). The exterior geometry of the BIMs defines the training target and contains no people or vehicles (Figure 4; Appendix B.1). Inference. sections.title: 4.3 ABLATIONS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: Parent initialization. Each finer level starts its flow sampling from the parents prediction noised to ts instead of pure noise (Section 3.2). We compare our default ts = 0.8 with ts = 0.9 and ts = 1 at every finer level (Figure 5(a)). At ts = 1, the finer levels start from pure noise and inherit only the cell placement. On the large ScanNet++ scenes with 32 views, lowering ts improves every metric and reduces the Chamfer distance by 80%. Results with 256 views are in Appendix G.1. Figure 5(b) shows city block. Overlapping cells keep neighboring surfaces continuous, but information from distant cells barely reaches cell, and the roof is not visible from the street. Without the parent, the roof breaks into fragments above the building. With the parent, all cells start from the same coarse building, and the roof stays in place. Image conditioning. Figure 6 compares, at the finest level, the GenRecon-style conditioner, our voxel-queried attention (Section 3.4), and the latter with the ConvNeXt branch, which adds pixellevel detail. The baseline bilinearly samples DINO features at projected voxel centers, which loses detail finer than token. On ScanNet++, voxel-queried attention alone is on par with the baseline, and the ConvNeXt branch substantially improves every metric. On the human capture, the baseline over-smooths the hair, the nose, and the shirt wrinkles. Voxel-queried attention recovers strands of hair, and the ConvNeXt branch sharpens them further and adds the shirt buttons. Appendix G.2 shows further qualitative results. Inference time. On large ScanNet++ scenes, single H200 takes 17 (L1) and 89 (L2) minutes per scene, comparable to per-scene optimization but slower than feed-forward methods (Appendix H).

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: We have presented T3lescope, generative reconstruction framework that applies single fixedresolution 3D generator across scene scales through an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade. The coarse level establishes globally consistent layout, finer levels recover surface detail, and cellindependent multi-scale image conditioning gives every cell images at the resolution it needs. On ScanNet++, Tanks and Temples, and city blocks, T3lescope outperforms the generative baseline and is competitive with or better than feed-forward and per-scene optimization methods.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Since T3lescope does not fit the input images pixel by pixel, its surfaces can be slightly offset from the observations, which lowers the F-score at tight thresholds when views are dense. Its cost grows with the number of cells and cascade levels, so sampling large scenes at high resolution remains slow, and it assumes posed images. Moreover, it does not work on distant objects in unbounded scenes (Appendix A.5). In future work, we plan to reduce the sampling cost by distilling the flow models into few-step samplers and to extend T3lescope to unbounded scenes.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our city-block images are taken on public streets and show passers-by and vehicles. In the released data, people and license plates are masked, and the released 3D Gaussian Splatting models and BIM meshes contain no people (Appendix B.1). The five people in our in-house human capture consented to being recorded. All other datasets are public and used under their own terms.

sections.content: B.1 DATASETS ScanNet++. We evaluate the 50 validation scenes of ScanNet++ (Yeshwanth et al., 2023) and divide them by the volume of the ground-truth bounding box into small and large split of 25 scenes each. We use the undistorted DSLR images at 1752 1168 as inputs and choose the 32and 256-view sets by farthest-point sampling of the camera centers among the training frames not flagged as bad. For the scenes with fewer than 256 frames, 12 in the small split and 9 in the large split, we use all of them. The ground truth is the mesh reconstructed from the laser scans, with its anonymized regions removed. Tanks and Temples. We evaluate six scenes of Tanks and Temples (Knapitsch et al., 2017). As for ScanNet++, the 16-, 32-, and 256-view sets are chosen by farthest-point sampling of the camera centers. truck has only 251 images and uses all of them in the 256-view setting. We extract the frames from the 4K videos provided by the dataset and undistort them to match the official COLMAP reconstruction, which gives images of approximately 3920 2180 (4K). For fair comparison with the baselines, the main paper uses these images downsampled by two to approximately 1960 1090 (2K), and Appendix A.2 reports additional results with the 4K images. The ground truth is the official laser scan with its crop volume and alignment. City blocks. Our city-block dataset contains 41 blocks with 248 buildings and 139,893 posed images at 9504 6336. We split it geographically into 38 training blocks with 220 buildings and 126,068 images, and three held-out evaluation blocks with 28 buildings and 13,825 images. The blocks range from 42 22 to 156 137 in horizontal extent, and the buildings are 23 to 172 tall. All images are captured with handheld camera at walking height, about 1 to 2 above the ground. We register the images using RealityScan and an in-house SfM pipeline, and align the reconstruction to laser scan of the block to obtain metric scale. The exterior BIM of each building is modeled in the coordinate frame of the same scan. The cameras and the BIM are therefore aligned without any further registration. We use the mesh derived from the BIM as the ground truth. It represents building exteriors, vegetation, and street furniture down to signs and traffic cones, but not people or vehicles. Each image is accompanied by masks of the sky, people, and vehicles. We will release the evaluation split, including the images, 3D Gaussian Splatting model of each block, and the BIM meshes. For evaluation, each held-out block is reconstructed from 256 of its images, sampled at uniform stride over the capture sequence. B.2 METRICS 3D metrics. Let and denote the points sampled from the predicted mesh and the ground truth, respectively, following each protocol (Appendix B.3). The Chamfer distance (CD) is the average of the mean nearest-neighbor distances from to and from to , in meters and without truncation. Precision and recall at threshold τ are the fractions of points in and in whose nearest neighbor in the other set lies within τ , and the F-score F@τ is their harmonic mean, with τ in centimeters. Normal consistency (NC) is the mean absolute cosine similarity between the normal of each point in and and that of its nearest neighbor in the other set, with pairs more than 20 cm apart counted as zero. 2D metrics. We follow the 2D metrics of GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026). We render depth and normal maps of the predicted and ground-truth meshes and compute the errors on the pixels covered by both. We report the mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) of depth in meters, the absolute relative error (AbsRel) mean ˆz z/z, and the squared relative error (SqRel) mean(ˆz z)2/z, where ˆz and are the predicted and ground-truth depths. Ang is the mean angular error in degrees between the rendered normals, which are interpolated from area-weighted vertex normals. Completeness (Comp) is the fraction of pixels covered by the ground truth that are also covered by the prediction. For depth, the main paper reports MAE and AbsRel, and Table 3 additionally reports RMSE and SqRel.

sections.content: B.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOLS ScanNet++. Although ScanNet++ registers the camera poses to the ground-truth mesh, the registration leaves residual errors on some scenes that are not negligible at the F@2 threshold. We therefore rigidly align the ground-truth mesh to the COLMAP sparse points of each scene with ICP before evaluation. This alignment is shared by all methods. We compute the 2D metrics following GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026), rendering both meshes from the cameras of the official test split, invalidating masked pixels, and pooling the errors over all pixels of all frames. As its evaluation code is not released, we reimplement it based on the paper. For the 3D metrics, the main paper uses the virtual-scan protocol of GaussianWrapping (Gomez et al., 2026), which scores only the surfaces that the cameras see and the ground truth contains. Unlike the original protocol, which uses all cameras of the capture, we use up to 300 held-out cameras chosen by farthest-point sampling among the frames that are neither input views of the run nor flagged as bad. We cast only the rays that hit the ground truth against the prediction, so missing surface lowers recall and surface outside the ground truth is never scored. Table 4 also reports the 3D evaluation protocol of GenRecon, which samples points uniformly over the complete meshes after discarding predicted triangles farther than 15 cm from the ground truth. We run its released code with four million points per mesh instead of 200,000 to reduce sampling noise. Since the ground truth misses windows, mirrors, ceilings, and surfaces behind furniture, this protocol cannot distinguish hole in the ground truth from hole in the prediction. Tanks and Temples. We use the virtual-scan protocol of GaussianWrapping. The protocol takes the points seen from all cameras of the official trajectory, crops them to the official volume, and aligns them to the ground truth by the released transform refined with ICP. F@τ uses the official per-scene threshold τ of 3 mm for ignatius, 5 mm for caterpillar and truck, 10 mm for barn and meetingroom, and 25 mm for courthouse. The main paper reports CD divided by τ to average over scenes, and Table 5 reports the per-scene CD in meters. On both ScanNet++ and Tanks and Temples, all methods are scored by the same implementation. Since our meshes can reach hundreds of millions of triangles, we implement custom rendering and evaluation script that handles such meshes without decimation. City blocks. As the BIM ground truth covers complete building exteriors, we compare the complete meshes rather than only the surfaces seen by the cameras. We crop only the reconstructions to the ground-truth footprint, the ground-plane projection of the ground-truth mesh, to remove their surroundings outside the block. Since NC counts only pairs within 20 cm, on this dataset it mainly reflects how much of the surface is recovered. B.4 BASELINES All baselines receive the same input views, camera poses, and intrinsics, and are evaluated on the meshes they produce. We use the official implementations and checkpoints. On ScanNet++ and Tanks and Temples, our method and the per-scene optimization methods take the input images at full resolution on ScanNet++ and at 2K on Tanks and Temples. The feed-forward methods and GenRecon resize them to the resolution expected by each model. The rows marked 4K in Table 5 instead give our method the higher-resolution images of Tanks and Temples. On city blocks, our method takes the original 9504 6336 images, whereas the baselines take undistorted images downsampled to 1920 1280. All methods are also given the extent of the block from the ground truth. 2DGS (Huang et al., 2024) uses depth ratio of 1 and distortion weight of 10 on ScanNet++ and city blocks, and the released settings on Tanks and Temples, with the masks applied to the photometric loss on city blocks. MILo (Guedon et al., 2025) uses the released fast configuration, with its preset for indoor scenes on ScanNet++ and the released evaluation settings on Tanks and Temples. GaussianWrapping (Gomez et al., 2026) uses the released training and mesh extraction settings. CityGaussianV2 (Liu et al., 2025) uses the released street-scene configuration, which trains coarse model and fine-tunes 2 2 partitions before merging them, with depth supervision from Depth Anything V2 (Yang et al., 2024) and the masks.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: DA3 (Lin et al., 2026) uses DA3-GIANT-1.1 conditioned on the input poses and intrinsics and processes all views in single forward pass, so that one scale converts the depth to meters. On ScanNet++, each image is split into four virtual cameras with narrower fields of view. MapAnything (Keetha et al., 2026) uses the released model conditioned on the input poses and intrinsics. Murre (Guo et al., 2025) uses the released settings, with sparse depth from the COLMAP points, or from the RealityScan export on city blocks. GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026) partitions the scene into overlapping chunks placed from the COLMAP sparse points, generates each chunk with TRELLIS.2-based generative model conditioned on the input images, and aggregates the overlapping latents into single mesh. We run its released code in the ScanNet++ mode with the default settings, conditioning on all input views. Mesh extraction. MILo, GaussianWrapping, and GenRecon output meshes directly. The other methods produce depth maps, which we fuse by TSDF fusion in Open3D (Zhou et al., 2018) with the ground-truth poses, keeping the 50 largest connected components. The voxel size, truncation, and maximum depth are 1 cm, 4 cm, and 4.5 on ScanNet++, following GenRecon, and 5 cm, 8 cm, and 200 on city blocks. On Tanks and Temples, we use the original per-scene settings of 2DGS. For 2DGS on ScanNet++, we use the voxel size of 0.6 cm and truncation of 2.4 cm that its authors use for large Tanks and Temples scenes. For CityGaussianV2, pixels with opacity below 0.5 are discarded before fusion. On city blocks, we mask the depth and crop the volume to the ground-truth extent enlarged by 10 m. Since Murre aligns each view to its own sparse depth, overlapping views are not made consistent, and on city blocks its fused mesh covers only small part of the ground truth  (Table 6)  .

sections.content: The full inference procedure for one scene is as follows. The subsections below describe the generator (Appendix C.1), its training (Appendix C.2), the scene-wide blending (Appendix C.3), the transfer between levels (Appendix C.4), and the cell sizes and extents (Appendix C.5). 1. For each level = 0, . . . , 1, with cell edge length sl = s0/2l: (a) Place the cells. At level 0, they cover the scene extent; at finer levels, they cover the surface predicted by the parent (Appendices C.5 and C.4). (b) Select the conditioning views and tiles for each cell (Appendix D.3). (c) Encode the tiles selected at this level into the tile bank, encoding each tile only once even if selected by multiple cells (Appendix D.2). (d) Run the SS stage on the scene-wide SS latent grid with MultiDiffusion, starting from noise at level 0 and from the noised parent latent at finer levels, and decode the predicted occupancy (cid:98)O(l). (e) Run the mesh stage on the active voxels of (cid:98)O(l) with MultiDiffusion. (f) Unless is the finest level, decode the shape latent up to resolution 2R and encode the blocks of the child cells as their inherited SS latents. 2. Decode the shape latent of the finest level, and optionally of other levels (Appendix F.2), into mesh with margin-based chunk decoding (Appendix F.1). C.1 TWO-STAGE 3D FLOW BACKBONE Our generator follows the two-stage design of TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026). It operates on one cell in canonical cell coordinates (Appendix C.2) and is conditioned on the posed images that observe the cell (Section 3.1). The SS stage generates the occupancy {0, 1}R3 of the cell with = 64, where active voxels (O = 1) contain surface geometry. The mesh stage then generates shape latent on the active voxels, which the shape VAE decoder converts into triangle mesh at 5123 resolution. Both stages are latent flow-matching models. The SS latent of an occupancy is x0 = ASS(ESS(O)), where ESS is the SS VAE encoder and ASS normalizes latents using the mean and standard deviation of the training latents. The shape latent is obtained from the ground-truth mesh by the shape VAE encoder. We keep both pretrained VAEs frozen (Appendix E.1) and train only the two flow models.

With half-cell stride, the weights of overlapping cells sum to one along each axis. The SS latent grid is dense, whereas the shape latent grid is sparse and holds only the active voxels; we apply the same averaging to both. We apply classifier-free guidance within each cell before blending: each cell combines its conditional and unconditional velocities and takes an Euler step, and we blend the updated latents of the cells with Equation 4. Since all cells start from the same grid, this is equivalent to blending the guided velocities. We use the overlapping half-stride cells only for blending. For mesh decoding, we use nonoverlapping base lattice to decode each region once without duplicated surfaces (Appendix F.1). Cell ordering, random seeds, and view selection are deterministic within run. C.4 PARENT-TO-CHILD GEOMETRY TRANSFER The shape VAE decoder upsamples shape latent through subdivision stages that each double the resolution. For the parent level, we run the decoder only up to resolution 2R. Because child cell has half the edge length of its parent, it spans exactly an R3 block of this grid, which we crop without spatial resampling. We encode the block with the SS VAE encoder to obtain the inherited SS latent x(l+1) of Section 3.2. For general power-of-two ratio between the parent and child edge lengths, 0 we stop at the stage of resolution rR instead. Because the child inherits its SS latent directly from the parents subdivision output rather than from the parent mesh, we extract intermediate meshes only when needed (e.g., when combining multiple levels, Appendix F.2) and skip them otherwise. Because the SS flow starts from ts rather than = 1, it requires fewer Euler steps. The parent also determines child cell placement: we keep child cell only if it intersects the parents predicted occupancy (cid:98)O(l), dilated by one parent SS voxel so that regions narrowly missed at the coarse level can still be recovered. Without this guidance, the location of the surface would be unknown, and fine cells would have to fill the entire scene volume at much higher cost. The DA3 points used to place the coarsest cells cannot take this role at finer levels: DA3 predicts points only for regions observed in the images, so in wide scenes with sparse views it misses surfaces that the coarse level can still generate. Parent-guided placement is used even at ts = 1, where noise replaces the inherited latent. C.5 CELL SIZES AND EXTENTS ScanNet++ and the city blocks use metric coordinates: in both, the camera poses are aligned to laser scans (Appendix B.1). On these datasets, cell edge lengths are specified in meters: 4, 2, and 1 on ScanNet++, and 80, 40, 20, and 10 on city blocks. The poses for Tanks and Temples and the three real-world captures (garden from Mip-NeRF 360, coffee martini from N3DV (Li et al., 2022), and our in-house human capture) come from SfM and have no metric scale. We rescale camera translations so that the median distance from the cameras to their centroid equals target value: 6 or 8 on Tanks and Temples, 1 on coffee martini, and 4 on garden and the human capture. Cell sizes are defined in these normalized units: 4, 2, and 1 units on Tanks and Temples, garden, and coffee martini, and 2.8, 1.4, and 0.7 units on the human capture. The coarsest cells cover horizontal extent and height range. The height range is computed from DA3 points for each scene (Appendix D.3) and is capped at 8 and 4 units on garden and the human capture, respectively. The horizontal extent is also computed from DA3 points on ScanNet++, meetingroom (Tanks and Temples), and coffee martini. City blocks use the footprint of the ground-truth mesh, while the remaining Tanks and Temples scenes and the human capture use the convex hull of the camera trajectory. On garden, cascade levels cover nested squares with halfwidths of 16, 8, and 4 units around the camera centroid, and their meshes are combined as described in Appendix F.2.

sections.content: D.1 VOXEL-QUERIED IMAGE ATTENTION This section details the voxel-queried image attention introduced in Section 3.4. It replaces the image cross-attention in every transformer block of both flows. In the mesh flow, each voxel attends to two types of image features: DINOv3 tokens around its projection in each view, and ConvNeXt features sampled at the projection. Below, we first contrast this design with pixel-aligned conditioning, and then describe the DINO branch (projection, geometric encoding, and attention), the ConvNeXt branch, and the variant used in the SS flow. Difference from pixel-aligned conditioning. Pixel-aligned generators sample one feature per view at the voxel projection and combine views before the 3D network. This design has two limitations in our setting. The first is resolution. DINO token covers 16 16-pixel patch; thus, features sampled from the token grid, even with bilinear interpolation, lack direct information finer than 16 pixels, which is insufficient for reconstructing fine mesh details. Pixal3D (Li et al., 2026a) upsamples DINO features to image resolution before sampling. For 512 512 tile, the upsampled 1,024-channel BF16 feature map requires 5122 1024 2 bytes = 0.5 GiB per view, (6) and 64 views require 32 GiB. MultiDiffusion evaluates every cell at every flow step, so features exceeding GPU memory must be recomputed at every evaluation. The second is view aggregation. Pixal3D averages sampled features over views, and GenRecon (Schmid et al., 2026) replaces the average with learned aggregator conditioned solely on image features. In both approaches, the view weights are independent of the voxel feature. Our attention addresses both limitations. For resolution, the attention score receives the offset from the voxel projection to each token center, preserving the sub-token position without upsampling. Shallow ConvNeXt feature maps provide image detail finer than 16 pixels at about 1% of the memory of upsampled DINO features. Both features are small enough to keep in memory for all views, so we compute them once and reuse them across cells and flow steps. For aggregation, we keep the tokens of all views separate until the attention step and use the current voxel feature as the query, so that the view weights depend on the voxel feature. sections.title: E TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: We train two models sharing the same architecture: general-scene model evaluated on ScanNet++, Tanks and Temples, and real-world captures, and city-scale model specialized for our city-block dataset. Both models start from the same initialization (Appendix E.1) and shared multi-view pretraining on TexVerse (Appendix E.2), differing only in their final scene-level fine-tuning data (Appendices E.3 and E.4). Both employ the same inference procedure (Appendix C). The remaining subsections detail scale and rotation augmentations (Appendix E.5) and optimization settings (Appendix E.6). E.1 MODEL INITIALIZATION Both flows are initialized from the official TRELLIS.2 weights. The SS flow retains the original 30-block architecture. For the mesh flow, we prune the 30-block backbone down to 15 transformer blocks by removing the blocks that affect its output the least, reducing the denoiser from approximately 1.3B to 655M parameters while preserving the hidden dimension, attention heads, and latent resolution of the retained blocks. To recover from pruning, we fine-tune the pruned mesh flow with the official single-image conditioning for 50k steps on 16 H200 GPUs with learning rate of 3 105. The voxel-queried image attention and the ConvNeXt branch are subsequently trained during image-conditioned multi-view training. We freeze the pretrained SS and shape VAEs, which encode the clean SS and shape targets and decode generated latents. We update only the two flow networks and their conditioning layers during training. E.2 SHARED MULTI-VIEW PRETRAINING After initialization, we train both flows on multi-view renderings of TexVerse (Zhang et al., 2025). This stage adapts the single-object generators, alongside the new conditioning modules, to posed multi-view inputs. The resulting checkpoint serves as the starting point for scene-level fine-tuning (Appendices E.3 and E.4). Training follows curriculum over mesh resolution and the number of randomly sampled conditioning views. The mesh flow is trained first with 4 views at mesh resolution 2563, then with 4 views at 5123, and finally with 16 views at 5123. The SS flow, whose occupancy targets have resolution of 643, is trained with 4 and subsequently 16 views. Conditioning images are rendered or cropped to 512 512. E.3 GENERAL-SCENE FINE-TUNING Starting from the TexVerse checkpoint (Appendix E.2), we fine-tune both flows of the general-scene model on multi-scale scene data. In addition to the single-room scene datasets SAGE-10K (Xia

E.4 CITY-SCALE FINE-TUNING The city-scale model is fine-tuned from the TexVerse checkpoint (Appendix E.2) on our city-block dataset (Appendix B.1), which pairs ground-level photographs of urban blocks with mesh targets derived from BIMs. It uses the same representations, voxel-queried image conditioning, multi-scale cell training, and inference procedure as the general-scene model, differing only in the fine-tuning data to accommodate urban blocks and building exteriors. E.5 SCALE AND ROTATION AUGMENTATION OF CELLS We augment training cells in both scale and orientation.

sections.content: Scale. We assign each room or house scene one of the two scale ladders {1, 2, 4} and {1.5, 3, 6} and partition it into cells of those sizes, which gives six cell sizes across the dataset. Because scene yields far more small cells than large ones, we sample cells with the scale-balanced scheme of Appendix C.2 to avoid over-representing small cells. Rotation. We rotate each cell independently of its scale in two ways. First, we rotate the cell about the vertical axis by uniformly sampled angle and tilt the vertical axis by up to 10. We sample the tilt angle from distribution concentrated near zero, which keeps most cells nearly upright while making the model robust to camera poses that are not perfectly level. Second, we apply rotations by multiples of 90 about the vertical axis alongside reflection flips, yielding eight discrete orientations per cell. The same transform is applied to the target geometry and the camera poses, and reflections also flip the images. Because these eight discrete transforms only permute the voxel grid, we apply them directly to the dual-grid representation of TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026) instead of recomputing it from the mesh. We still re-encode the SS and shape latents of each transformed cell, because neither VAE encoder is equivariant to these transforms. Because the tile bank is independent of cells (Appendix D.2), these augmentations leave the image processing unchanged: all cell variants access the same tiles and differ only in their relative camera transforms. E.6 OPTIMIZATION SETTINGS Both flows are optimized using AdamW with constant learning rate, weight decay of 0.01, β = (0.9, 0.95), and ϵ = 108, with BF16 mixed precision and per-GPU batch size of 8. The learning rate is 104 during the 4-view phases of the mesh flow, 5 105 in other pretraining phases, and 105 during scene-level fine-tuning. For classifier-free guidance, the conditioning input is dropped with probability 0.1. We set σmin = 105 in the flow path of Equation 2. TexVerse pretraining (Appendix E.2) runs on 16 to 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs for approximately 80k steps for the SS flow and 200k steps for the mesh flow in total. Scene-level fine-tuning (Appendices E.3 and E.4) runs for 25,000 steps per flow on 8 H200 GPUs.

sections.title: F SCALABLE MESH DECODING
sections.content: F.1 MARGIN-BASED CHUNK DECODING AND STITCHING We decode each cascade level into unified scene mesh. Decoding cells independently would truncate the shape VAE receptive field at cell boundaries, producing visible seams. Instead, we assemble the shape tokens across all cells into single sparse tensor for the level. Because cells overlap by 50% during MultiDiffusion (Appendix C.3), we select every other cell along each axis to partition the volume without overlap. Because decoding the entire level at once exceeds GPU memory, we process it in blocks of 43 cells. Each block is padded with 4-voxel latent margin from its neighbors, so that voxels near the block boundary are decoded with their surroundings. Each block outputs only the mesh faces belonging to its interior region, preventing duplicate faces between adjacent blocks. We merge the copies of each boundary vertex produced by adjacent blocks into single vertex, identifying them by their integer voxel coordinates. The blocks thus join into one mesh without duplicate faces or open seams. F.2 COMBINING CASCADE LEVELS In object-centered captures such as Mip-NeRF 360 (Barron et al., 2022), cameras orbit central subject observed closely from many angles, while the background is seen only from afar. Because the background appears too small in the images to show fine detail, we do not reconstruct it at the finest resolution: we run the coarsest level over the full bounding volume and restrict successive refinement levels to concentric squares centered on the subject. For the garden scene in Figure 1, we employ three cascade levels, with each finer level covering half the horizontal extent of its predecessor. Each level yields an independent mesh, which we merge hierarchically. Because finer meshes provide higher fidelity in the central region, we remove coarse faces whose centroids fall within the boundary of the next finer level, and combine the remaining outer ring with the finer mesh. sections.title: H INFERENCE TIME
sections.content: Table 13 reports the inference time for each cascade level on five large ScanNet++ scenes with 32 input views on single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Because each level halves the cell size, the number of cells and the total computation can grow by roughly 8 per level, and by more depending on the cell layout. In practice, the number of cells grows from 31 to 470 to 2,490, and runtime increases by 8.2 from level 0 to level 1 but only by 4.7 from level 1 to level 2, because finer levels allocate cells only where the parent level detects surfaces. Reconstruction up to level 1 takes an average of 17 minutes per scene, and up to level 2 takes 89 minutes, which is comparable to per-scene optimization methods. Flow sampling in the SS and mesh stages accounts for most of the runtime at all levels, whereas view selection, tile preparation, and parent transfer require less than 3 minutes combined. Peak GPU memory usage is 79 GiB at the finest level. Table 13: Inference time per cascade level on ScanNet++.
